name: Tar
label: Touch and Go
lede: A DeKalb hardcore band moved to Chicago, asked a local luthier for guitars they couldn't break, and got aluminum. Seven years and six records on Amphetamine Reptile and Touch and Go later, worn out from the road, Tar finished one last album and called it.

eras.title: Blatant Dissent grows up
eras.text: Tar started as a hardcore band called Blatant Dissent at Northern Illinois University in DeKalb, good enough for John Peel to play on BBC radio. When the new songs stopped sounding like hardcore, the band moved to Chicago, added a second guitarist and took a new name.

years.src: Punk Database · John Peel Wiki · Wikipedia: Tar
years.h: Mark Zablocki joins Blatant Dissent on guitar
years.p: Singer-guitarist John Mohr and drummer Mike Greenlees had started the band at NIU with bassist Tim Mescher. Zablocki comes in after guitarist Bruce Halverson leaves.
years.xp: Blatant Dissent's records had already made it to [[John Peel|e4dec348-ad10-43b6-a2b1-c22aab890675]], who played them on his show and kept playing the band after the name change.

years.h: The new songs don't sound like Blatant Dissent, so the band becomes Tar
years.p: The name change is official in April 1988. The first single, Play to Win, comes out that year on No Blow, Mohr's own label.

eras.title: Amphetamine Reptile, and guitars made of metal
eras.text: Minneapolis label Amphetamine Reptile put out Tar's first three records, two of them engineered by Steve Albini or Iain Burgess. Downstroked power chords, no solos, no lead guitar, and a melodic singer under it all. And the instruments looked like nothing else onstage.

years.src: Wikipedia: Tar · Punk Database · Trouser Press
years.h: Handsome is AmRep's first Tar record
years.p: A mini-album engineered by Steve Albini and Iain Burgess. It includes the band's own Static, a title that comes back in 1992.

years.src: Specimen Products: Chicago Tribune · Chicago Reader: Tar kick the dust
years.h: Mohr asks Ian Schneller for a guitar he can't destroy
years.p: Schneller, ex-Shrimp Boat guitarist and the one-man shop behind Specimen Products, builds Mohr a hollow aluminum body braced inside. The bass gets one too.
years.xp:
The Chicago Tribune's 1993 profile dates the request to about four years earlier, and has Mohr's reasoning in one line: "We thought metal might be nice." A Specimen instrument took six to seven months and cost $1,500 to $2,000.

The guitars turned up in Ministry's N.W.O. video and on the cover of Tar's Clincher.

years.h: Roundhouse gets Tar their first video
years.p: Out on Amphetamine Reptile in the US and Glitterhouse in Europe. The video is for Les Paul Worries.

years.h: Tom Zaluckyj takes over bass from Tim Mescher
years.p: Mescher heads off to Snailboy. Zaluckyj arrives in time for an AmRep package tour of Europe with [[Helmet|582fee78-d934-4603-9f5c-1729e0ca36b7]], Surgery and God Bullies.
years.xp: The tour was filmed for the Jettisoundz video Ugly American Overkill. Punk Database puts Zaluckyj's arrival in 1990; Wikipedia says early 1991.

years.h: Four songs for John Peel at Maida Vale
years.p: In their first week in Europe, Tar record Viaduct Removal, Walking the King, Ballad of the Storyteller and Play to Win. Peel airs the session on July 7.
years.xp: It was the band's only Peel session. It finally came out on vinyl in 2013, on Chunklet's 1988–1995 double LP.

years.h: Jackson ends the AmRep run
years.p: The third and last Amphetamine Reptile release. By now Mohr's guitar and Zaluckyj's bass are both Specimen aluminum.

eras.title: Touch and Go, then over and out
eras.text: Majors came calling and Tar went to Touch and Go instead, put out two records in one year and toured on them relentlessly. Worn out by early 1994, the band agreed to stop, but only after one more album.

years.h: Slash and MCA call; Tar signs with Touch and Go
years.p: Wikipedia names Slash Records and MCA among the major labels that approached the band. Tar picks Corey Rusk's Chicago indie.

years.h: Tar and Jawbox swap songs called Static
years.p: A split single on Touch and Go and Dischord: Tar covers [[Jawbox|016fba14-1fc6-4986-86c2-2113ec9b28de]]'s Static, and Jawbox covers Tar's song with the same name.

years.src: Chicago Reader: Tar kick the dust · Specimen Products: Chicago Tribune
years.h: The aluminum guitars make the cover of Clincher
years.p: Tar's Touch and Go debut, a short EP. The Chicago Reader later wrote that the guitars had become the band's signature.

years.h: A few months later, a whole album: Toast
years.p: The second Tar record of 1993, followed by heavy touring. Writers compared the later records to [[Helmet|582fee78-d934-4603-9f5c-1729e0ca36b7]] and [[The Jesus Lizard|dfebd6c0-dae7-4cc8-a8e9-0dbaa382209f]]; Andrew Earles called Tar a smoothed-out Helmet.

years.cap: Mohr at the wheel of the band's van in Florida, summer 1993, with Arcwelder's van alongside
years.h: Exhausted, Tar agrees to one more album and out
years.p: After years of touring the band decides to break up but finish a last record first. The plan is nine months; it takes more than a year.

years.h: The last album says it in the title
years.p: Over and Out, on Touch and Go, is the band's sixth release. Trouser Press called it the aptly titled finale.

years.src: Punk Database · Wikipedia: Tar · Chicago Reader: Tar play
years.h: Mohr gives his guitar away after the last show at Lounge Ax
years.p: Tar's final set is at Lounge Ax in Chicago. When it's over, Mohr hands his guitar to someone in the room.
years.xp: The show was taped; it's on Bandcamp and on the 2021 Tar Box. Sources split on the date: Wikipedia says November 24, while the Bandcamp release and Punk Database say November 25.

eras.title: Out of storage, a few times
eras.text: Tar never really came back, but it kept turning up: a barbecue, a Shellac opening slot, a festival, a pressing plant's party. In between, the archive came out, 150 copies at a time.

years.h: A barbecue, then an opening slot for Shellac
years.p: Tar reunites for the PRF BBQ festival in Chicago, then later that year opens for [[Shellac|604f273a-d3c1-4b5b-ab83-99541f9368ea]] at Lincoln Hall.

years.cap: Mohr and his aluminum guitar at the Bottom Lounge, Chicago, July 2017
years.src: Chicago Reader: Tar kick the dust · Wikipedia: Tar
years.h: The aluminum comes back out at the Bottom Lounge
years.p: Tar plays All Tomorrow's Impeachments, a two-night festival at Chicago's Bottom Lounge. The Chicago Reader calls it most definitely a special occasion.

years.src: Wikipedia: Tar · Chicago Reader: Tar play
years.h: Tar Box collects the AmRep years and the last show
years.p: Four discs on No Blow and Chunklet: Handsome, Roundhouse, Jackson, a 1992 Lounge Ax set and the November 1995 farewell.

yt: Mohr plays and talks at Smashed Plastic, 2022
years.h: First show in five years, at the plant that pressed the box
years.p: Tar plays Smashed Plastic's first daylong festival in Chicago. The pressing plant made the Tar Box vinyl.

years.h: Mohr and Greenlees resurface as Deep Tunnel Project
years.p: Formed in 2021 with [[Silkworm|64c9ed9d-0b97-4e01-946c-2ef5f342e236]]'s Tim Midyett and Jeff Dean of [[The Bomb|a056d886-5706-4a49-813d-ada40be71c93]]. Their self-titled album is out on Comedy Minus One.
